extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate/graduate students and practitioners of classical mechanics
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and formal development of Newtonian mechanics: presenting principles (composition of motions, equilibrium, elasticity, lever laws), deriving formulae (momentum, impulse, work, energy), and explaining methodological and historical considerations for solving mechanical problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of motions / superposition in thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagine accelerations (and the small motions they produce) in each direction independently and compose them to obtain the resultant position and velocity after a small time interval; repeat for successive small intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the device of performing all small accelerated motions independently and composing velocities/positions to trace the motion; this is a foundational schematic method even when exact symbolic solutions are difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equilibrium criterion via neutralising accelerations
rubrics_metrics.description: If the accelerations of a mass (or several masses) collectively neutralise each other, the mass(es) are in equilibrium and will move uniformly with their initial velocities; if initial velocities are zero, rest obtains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat equilibrium as the special case where net acceleration is zero; in practice neglect small tremors/disturbances when focusing on schematic equilibrium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivision of extended bodies into small portions
rubrics_metrics.description: When masses have considerable extension and no single line joins every two masses, divide the body into sufficiently small portions and draw lines of junction between portions; account for reciprocal relations of parts (e.g., elasticity, rigidity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model extended bodies as aggregates of small interacting parts to apply pairwise interactions; this justifies continuum/elastic theory and the rigid-body idealization as limiting cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elastic forces proportional to change of distance
rubrics_metrics.description: On alteration of distance between two parts of a mass, an acceleration is observed proportional to that alteration; increased distances diminish and diminished distances increase due to this acceleration (elastic response).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use linear proportionality (Hooke-like behavior) as the schematic model for elasticity; note elastic forces arise only on deformation/contact in impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigid-body idealization / neglect of internal vibrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies for which mutual displacement of parts is evanescent may be treated as rigid bodies; with sufficient hardness vibrations can be neglected in analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify neglecting small internal oscillations when stiffness is large relative to forces of interest; explicitly state this approximation when moving from detailed elastic models to rigid-body mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for internal elastic counter-accelerations in columns
rubrics_metrics.description: In a vertical column under gravity, elastic forces between particles generate upward accelerations that balance downward gravitational acceleration leading to equilibrium; lower portions are more compressed than upper ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an exemplar of internal stresses producing equilibrium; recognize real bodies exhibit tremors but they are neglected in schematic equilibrium analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equation-manipulation method to decouple motions
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain differential equations for interacting masses, then use subtraction/addition or repeated differentiation to eliminate variables and derive equations for individual coordinates which can be integrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply algebraic elimination (subtract/add) to decouple coupled equations rather than always integrating the full system; choose the method that yields the clearest integrable form for the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of oscillatory motion in elastic systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Two masses connected elastically execute oscillatory motion symmetric about their centre of gravity; period (T = 2π sqrt(m/p)) decreases and amplitude decreases with increasing stiffness p; oscillations may be damped by resistance or initial configuration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing elastic interactions, compute periods and amplitudes; determine whether oscillations are negligible (hard bodies, high frequency, small excursion) or must be included (soft bodies or sustained oscillations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modelling lever as elastic triangular schema
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent a lever as masses at triangle vertices joined by elastic connections; alterations of sides/angles produce accelerations tending to restore original shape; from this Newtonian schema one can deduce lever laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat fulcrum as an immovable large mass (or elastically connected to very large masses) and neglect its motion; take small-altitude limits to recover standard lever geometry and relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism of distortion leading to rotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distortion of the triangular lever increases until accelerations of masses reach proportions equivalent to rotation about the fulcrum (no further distortion); at that stage the lever rotates as a rigid body with fixed acceleration relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the evolution of internal accelerations under distortion to determine when a rigid-body rotational mode replaces further deformation; derive the proportionality relations linking accelerations and arm lengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lever equilibrium: equal and opposite moments
rubrics_metrics.description: Two equal and opposite forces produce equilibrium when their moments with respect to the fulcrum are equal and opposite; compound forces combine by Varignon's parallelogram principle and the resultant passes through the fulcrum when moments cancel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce force systems to moments about the fulcrum; compound forces may be decomposed and recomposed using parallelogram constructions to verify equilibrium conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varignon's statics as a dynamical statics included in Newtonian view
rubrics_metrics.description: The Newtonian (dynamical) point of view includes Varignon's statics: starting from dynamical ideas and restricting to equilibrium yields the statics relations; certain abstract operations (e.g., translation of forces) are clearer dynamically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Newtonian dynamical reasoning to provide physical insight behind abstract statical operations; prefer the viewpoint that best illuminates the particular conceptual point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic method choice and economy of Newtonian principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Newtonian principles can in principle treat every mechanical phenomenon, in practice other methods (e.g., Huygenian) may solve specific problems more advantageously; do not insist on Newtonian approach dogmatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the method that gives the desired balance of insight and efficiency for the problem; demonstrate Newtonian reducibility at least once to show equivalence of methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental formulae and their interrelations
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic relations for uniformly accelerated motion and their mass-multiplied forms: v = φ t; m v = p (momentum); mv^2 = 2 p s (vis viva/work relations); m φ s = ? etc. These equations relate s, t, v, φ, m, p and can be arranged to answer different physical questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the appropriate combination of variables to answer determinate questions; recognize which variables must be supplied (e.g., to find force giving velocity one must also supply either distance s or time t).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding indeterminate problem formulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain questions are indeterminate unless sufficient quantities are specified; for example, asking 'what force f will impart velocity v to mass m' is indeterminate unless either distance s or time t is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly state what quantities are fixed/known when posing mechanical questions; inspect equations to ensure the problem has enough constraints to determine the unknown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and names: momentum, impulse, vis viva, work
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical and operational definitions: mv often called momentum (quantity of motion), ft called impulse (Belanger), mv^2 (vis viva/living force) tied to work/energy; ps associated with work; units (kilogram-metre) used for work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt precise terminology appropriate to context (momentum vs quantity of motion; kinetic energy vs vis viva) and be explicit about units used; note historical multiple usages and modern preferred terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish different measures of 'force' and their applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Cartesian measure (mv) and Leibnitzian measure (mv^2) each have justification in different contexts (momentum vs measure of effect in raising heights); neither should be conflated with Newtonian force; distinguish 'measure of force' from conservation statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing 'force' or 'measure of force', clarify the intended sense (momentum, kinetic energy, or dynamical force) and avoid conflating conservation of one quantity with properties of another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Units and systematic choice yet incomplete
rubrics_metrics.description: The important formulae were discovered early, but particular designations and a systematical set of mechanical units were introduced later and remained under refinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting formulae, also present consistent units and explain chosen conventions (e.g., kilogram-metre for work); acknowledge ongoing standardisation where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/contextual exposition to motivate definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain historical disputes (Descartes vs Leibnitz) and the experimental basis (Galileo, Huygens) to motivate why particular measures (momentum, vis viva) were proposed and how modern usage emerged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical narrative to clarify conceptual distinctions and justify adopted conventions; show how empirical tests decide between competing a priori claims.
